passage: Wednesday. Day 6 of the morning plan. Wake at 6:30 no matter what. Curtains open first, the light hits my face and it actually helps. Then ten minutes of stretches, a short walk round the block with Siddharth from next door, and breakfast at the table: idli today. Last week I tried to force bedtime to nine and just stared at the ceiling. This time I'm not fighting the night; I'm fixing the morning and letting the night catch up. Yesterday I fell asleep at 11:20, about forty minutes earlier than usual, without trying. Siddharth says the walk is the best part. I think it's the breakfast. Tomorrow same again, 6:30, curtains, walk, idli or poha. - Madhav

qa.q: At what time does Madhav wake up in the morning plan?
qa.a: Madhav wakes at 6:30 no matter what.

qa.q: How does Madhav feel about the new approach compared with forcing bedtime?
qa.a: Madhav feels more relaxed and hopeful, no longer fighting the night, and pleased that sleep came earlier without trying.

qa.q: What else could Madhav add if sleep still comes late, and why?
qa.a: Madhav could keep the light-and-walk morning going for another week and dim the room earlier at night, because a strong morning anchor helps the body clock more than forcing bedtime.

qa.q: How might Siddharth see the morning walk?
qa.a: Siddharth likely enjoys it as company and says the walk is the best part, though Madhav thinks it is the breakfast.

grounding: The student sets a fixed wake time, opens curtains for daylight, does light exercise and has breakfast, since a strong morning routine helps the body clock more than forcing an early bedtime.
